'''Cyril Hilsum''' (17 May 1925 – 23 September 2026) was a British physicist and academic.

Hilsum was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1983 for the inventiveness and leadership in introducing [[III-V semiconductor|III-V semiconductors]] into electronic technology.

==Education and career==
Hilsum entered [[Raine's Foundation School]] in 1936 as the middle of three brothers, leaving in 1943 after being accepted into [[University College London]], where he did his BSc. In 1945, he joined the [[Royal Naval Scientific Service]], moving in 1947 to the [[Admiralty Research Laboratory]].<ref name="fp"/> In 1950, he transferred again to the [[Services Electronics Research Laboratory]] (SERL) where he remained until 1964 before again moving, this time to the [[Royal Radar Establishment]].<ref name="fp"/> In 1974 he became [[Chief Scientific Officer]].<ref name=archivesit-20200117>{{cite web |url=https://archivesit.org.uk/interviews/cyril-hilsum-cbe/ |title=Interview with Cyril Hilsum CBE |last=Mori |first=Elisabetta |website=Archives of IT |date=17 January 2020 |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>

He won the [[Heinrich Welker Memorial Award]] in 1978,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iscs2007.org/index.php?Awards|title=Awards – ISCS2007|access-date=13 November 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090401014824/http://www.iscs2007.org/index.php?Awards|archive-date=1 April 2009|url-status=dead|website=International Symposium on Compound Semiconductors}}</ref> was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering]],<ref name="List of Fellows"/> a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1979 and an honorary member of the American [[National Academy of Engineering]].<ref name="fp"/>

In 1983, he was appointed chief scientist at [[Hirst Research Centre|GEC Hirst Research Centre]]. He was awarded the [[Max Born Prize]] in 1987, the 1988 [[Faraday Medal]], and from then until 1990 served as president of the [[Institute of Physics]]. In the [[1990 Queen's Birthday Honours]], he was appointed a [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE)<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=52173|pages=7–8|date=15 June 1990}}</ref> for "services to the Electrical and Electronics Industry".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npg.org.uk/collections/search/person/mp06516/cyril-hilsum|title=Cyril Hilsum (1925–) Physicist|access-date=30 January 2024|website=[[National Portrait Gallery (London)|National Portrait Gallery]]}}</ref> He was the subject of a photograph by [[Nick Sinclair]] in 1993 that is currently held by the [[National Portrait Gallery (London)|National Portrait Gallery]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npg.org.uk/collections/search/portrait/mw09509/Cyril-Hilsum|title=NPG P564(10) Cyril Hilsum|access-date=28 March 2019|website=[[National Portrait Gallery (London)|National Portrait Gallery]]}}</ref> In 1998, he was awarded the [[Richard Glazebrook Medal and Prize]] from the Institute of Physics, and is notable as the only scientist to hold both this and the Faraday Medal together.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://malvernscienceservices.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=91:professor-cyril-hilsum-cbe&catid=48:our-team&Itemid=89 |title=Professor Cyril Hilsum CBE |access-date=13 November 2008|website=Malvern Science Services}}{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

He served as a corporate research advisor for various entities, including [[Cambridge Display Technology]], the [[European Commission]] and [[Unilever]]. In 2007, he was awarded the [[Royal Society]]'s [[Royal Medal]] "for his many outstanding contributions and for continuing to use his prodigious talents on behalf of industry, government and academe to this day".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1dsunM9ukGLgaW3HdG9cvJ_QKd7pWjGI0qi_fCb1ROD4/pubhtml?gid=1640032608&single=true|title=Award winners : Royal Medal|access-date=30 January 2024|via=[[Google Sheets]]|publisher=[[Royal Society]]}}</ref>

Hilsum served as chairman of the scientific board for Peratech and was a visiting professor of physics at [[University College London]], as well as sitting on the [[Defence Scientific Advisory Council]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.peratech.com/board.php |title=Peratech Board Members |access-date=13 November 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090107041336/http://www.peratech.com/board.php |archive-date=7 January 2009|website=Peratech}}</ref> He also endorsed the [[Karen Burt]] Memorial Award, named after his daughter, which is awarded yearly by the [[Women's Engineering Society]] "to a woman engineer of high calibre who has newly attained full corporate membership and Chartered Engineer status through her relevant professional Institution and who has contributed to the promotion of the engineering profession".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wes.org.uk/?q=content/jane-wild-was-presented-karen-burt-memorial-award-wes-president-pam-wain|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815234809/http://www.wes.org.uk/?q=content%2Fjane-wild-was-presented-karen-burt-memorial-award-wes-president-pam-wain|url-status=dead|archive-date=15 August 2017|title=Jane Wild was presented with the Karen Burt Memorial Award by WES president Pam Wain|access-date=13 November 2008|df=dmy-all|website=[[Women's Engineering Society]]}}</ref> In 2006, he was made a Fellow of the ESSCIRC,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.esscirc.org/en/page/fellows.aspx|title=ESSCIRC – Fellows|access-date=13 November 2008|website=European Conference on Solid-State Circuits|archive-date=25 October 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081025062949/http://www.esscirc.org/en/page/fellows.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> and in 2007 wrote an obituary for [[Gareth Roberts (physicist)|Gareth Roberts]] for ''[[The Guardian]]''<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2007/mar/17/obituaries.guardianobituaries|title=Obituary: Sir Gareth Roberts|accessdate=13 November 2008 | work=[[The Guardian]] | date=17 March 2007 | first=Cyril | last=Hilsum|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260926224603/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2007/mar/17/obituaries.guardianobituaries|archive-date=2026-09-26}}</ref> and the Royal Society.<ref>{{Cite journal | last = Hilsum | first = C.| doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2011.0016 | title = Sir Gareth Gwyn Roberts. 16 May 1940 -- 6 February 2007 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | year = 2011 | volume = 57 | pages = 379–393 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

On 9 December 2025, Hilsum was given a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Electronics Weekly Elektra Awards,<ref>{{cite web |title=Electronics Weekly Elektra Awards |url=https://www.electronicsweekly.com/news/elektra-awards-news/elektra-awards-2025-the-winners-2025-12/ |website=Electronics Weekly |access-date=10 December 2025}}</ref> citing in particular his role in pioneering compound semiconductor technology and his research in LCD technology.

==Research==
[[File:Cyanobiphenyl LCD clock, RRE, 1973.jpg|thumb|Demonstration digital clock using cyanobiphenyl liquid crystals made at the [[Royal Radar Establishment]] in 1973]]
While working for the [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]], Hilsum helped develop commercial applications for [[gallium arsenide]], and was responsible for creating the UK's first [[semiconductor laser]]. He was one of the developers of the 
[[Ridley Watkins Hilsum theory|Ridley-Watkins-Hilsum theory]] that provided the theoretical basis of the transferred electron device, better known as the [[Gunn diode]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mwrf.com/Articles/Print.cfm?ArticleID=19913|title=Microwave Legends|work=Microwaves & RF|first=Nancy|last=Friedrich |date=October 2008|access-date=13 November 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714141532/http://www.mwrf.com/Articles/Print.cfm?ArticleID=19913|archive-date=14 July 2011}}</ref> and his research also helped form the basis of modern [[LCD]] technology,<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://www.lcd-displays-manufacturers.com/suserfiles/upload/lcd_history_blaze_display.pdf|title=The history of liquid-crystal displays|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121144533/http://www.lcd-displays-manufacturers.com/suserfiles/upload/lcd_history_blaze_display.pdf |archive-date=21 January 2013|url-status=dead|first=Hirohisa |last=Kawamoto|journal=Proceedings of the IEEE|volume=90|number=4|date=April 2002|pages=460–500 |doi=10.1109/JPROC.2002.1002521 |bibcode=2002IEEEP..90..460K }}</ref> bringing in over £100 million of royalties to the UK government.<ref name=telegraph-20260930>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2026/09/30/cyril-hilsum-liquid-crystals-flate-screen-tv-smartphone-mod/ |title=Obituary: Prof Cyril Hilsum, physicist behind the liquid crystals that led to flat-screen TVs and smartphones |website=The Telegraph |location=London |url-access=subscription |date=30 September 2026 |access-date=30 September 2026}}</ref>

Since 2006, the [[British Liquid Crystal Society]] has awarded the Hilsum Medal<ref name=blcs-hilsum>{{cite web |url=https://www.blcs.org.uk/?page_id=65 |title=Hilsum Medal |website=British Liquid Crystal Society |access-date=30 September 2026}}</ref> each year "to British candidates for overall contributions to liquid-crystal science and technology. The award is made to mid-career scientists who have made notable contributions to the subject over a number of years."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/news-articles/0804/08043004|title=Cyril Hilsum Medal awarded|publisher=University College London|date=30 April 2008|access-date=13 November 2008}}</ref><ref name=telegraph-20260930/>

==Personal life and death==
Cyril Hilsum was born on 17 May 1925.<ref name="fp">{{cite web|url=http://www.davidaspencer.com/oldraineians/pr030famousraineians.html |title=Famous personalities from Raine's Foundation School |access-date=13 November 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080616012837/http://www.davidaspencer.com/oldraineians/pr030famousraineians.html |archive-date=16 June 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was born in the East End of London and was the second of three sons of Jewish parents, Benjamin Hilsum, a street peddler, and his wife, Ada.<ref>https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/article/cyril-hilsum-obituary-death-6p0sbhpss accessed 15 October 2026</ref> He married Betty Hilsum, with whom he had two daughters, [[Lindsey Hilsum|Lindsey]], a news correspondent for [[Channel 4]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/broadcast-media-lp7d9f9hkcr|url-access=subscription|title=Broadcast media|access-date=13 November 2008 | location=London | website=[[The Times]] | date=5 January 2004}}</ref> and [[Karen Burt]], an engineer who died in 1997 and in whose name Hilsum endowed a [[Women's Engineering Society]] memorial award.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bcs.org/server.php?show=nav.5929|title=Karen Burt Award |website=[[British Computer Society]]|access-date=13 November 2008|archive-date=5 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705043141/http://www.bcs.org/server.php?show=nav.5929|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=About the Award |url=https://www.bcs.org/category/8186 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705164649/http://www.bcs.org/server.php?show=nav.8186 |archive-date=5 July 2010 |publisher=British Computer Society}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Karen Burt Memorial Award |url=https://www.wes.org.uk/karen-burt-memorial-award |access-date=1 November 2026 |website=The Women's Engineering Society}}</ref>

Hilsum [[centenarian|turned 100]] in 2025,<ref>{{cite web | title=Former IOP president Cyril Hilsum celebrates 100th birthday | date=22 May 2025 | url=https://physicsworld.com/a/former-iop-president-cyril-hilsum-celebrates-100th-birthday/ }}</ref> and died in London on 23 September 2026, at the age of 101.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Banks |first=Michael |date=2026-09-25 |title=Cyril Hilsum, former GEC research boss and Institute of Physics president, dies aged 101 |url=https://physicsworld.com/cyril-hilsum-former-gec-research-boss-and-institute-of-physics-president-dies-aged-101/ |access-date=2026-09-26 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> Michael S. Rosenwald's ''[[The New York Times|New York Times]]'' obituary remarked that he had "survived into his 11th decade by avoiding fresh vegetables and subsisting largely on [[TV dinners]], chocolate and red wine".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rosenwald |first=Michael S. |date=1 November 2026 |title=That Giant HDTV That Fits in Your Living Room? Thank Cyril Hilsum |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/technology/cyril-hilsum-dead.html |access-date=1 November 2026 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

==Works==

* Liquid Crystals, C. Hilsum, Cambridge Univ Press (1985), {{ISBN|0-521-30465-2}}
* Device Physics (Vol. 4 of Handbook on Semiconductors), C. Hilsum and T.S. Moss (Editors), 1244 pages, Publ. JAI Press (1993) {{ISBN|0-444-88813-6}}
* Communications After AD2000, C. Hilsum, D.E.N. Davies, A.W. Rudge (Editors), Chapman & Hall, (1993), {{ISBN|0-412-49550-3}}
